chapter: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
title: The blackjack game that lost his suit money, and the end of his gambling
summary: Paid at the Adams Theatre in Newark, he dealt blackjack to Lucky and others, lost his pay, and came home to tell his wife there would be no suits.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: But you know, when we were traveling with the Ink Spots, there were some funny things that used to happen there with the gambling. I remember one morning, I was leaving to go to the Adams Theatre in Newark, New Jersey; we were playing over there. So, I had been broke for about 8 months, so I

finally got myself out of debt, and my wife said, 'Well, we have all the bills paid up, so when you get paid today, you can go down to F&F -- that was where all the musicians used to go to get their suits made. In New York. So she said to go down to F&F and have you a couple of suits made.

So I said okay. So, I go to the theatre, and we played the first show. Well, just before I went onstage, an old friend of mine came by -- Davey Tough, Davie Duff, a drummer -- he came by, and I sent the valet out to get a bottle for us, and while he went to get this bottle, they called 'all on', so I had to go onstage.

We got paid right after that show. I couldn't wait; I was the first one, because every theatre we played, we had a room set up where we all would go in this room and either shoot crap or play blackjack. So I ran down to this room and grabbed the cards, and said, 'My bank was $175' -- that is what I was making at that time. So there was Lucky, Taft Smith, Deak Deke Watson and Bill Kinney -- these were the four guys I had to deal to.
The three Ink Spots and the bandleader.
The band leader, and the saxophone player named Taft Smith.
Yeah.
No, it was two Ink Spots, the saxophone player, Taft Smith, and the band leader, Lucky Millinder. So Lucky took $25,
Taft took $25, Deak took $25, and Bill Kinney, who was a big time gambler, said "Deak deal the rest of it in here."

So, I dealt the cards around, and we had a thing called "sweating the cards" -- you'd take them and squeeze them and you'd peep at them and go through all kinds of things just to see if you could squeeze the 21 out of them when you look at them.

So I got mine and I sweat them and I looked at them, and I got a hard 15 to hit, because everybody either hit and waited, and the man on the end, who was Bill Kinney, who had $100, was a guy that I was worried about -- this was the man I wanted to beat.
So nobody busted out?

Nobody busted out. And I got a hard 15 to hit. So I said, well, I'll go in the deck, and I pulled this card off and I put it in with the two that I had, and I'm looking at the guys who are making the speech and sweating the cards as they talked, and I finally looked and here was a four spot. So I got 19 -- which they called a dead man's hand.
Yeah ...

Anyway, I beat Taft, and I beat Deak, no, I beat Taft and I beat Lucky, and I pushed with Deak and I pushed Bill Kinney. So now I got a second time to deal around. Lucky took $25, Taft took $25, Deak took
Kinney said, $25, Bill said to Deal the rest here." Dealed the cards around; opened up my hand, I got 17 to hit.
You got 17?
Yeah, so I look at my 17, I laid it down and say, 'Well, fellows, what you want?' -- and I turned around and I hit Lucky; I hit Lucky first, and I bust him out; I hit Tab -- he beat me.
He beat you because he didn't know yet.
Huh?
He didn't know yet.
I mean, I hit him and he waited. I hit Deak, and he waited, and Bill Kinney waited, and I got 17. So I turned my hand out; I beat Lucky -- Deak beats me; Tab beat me and Bill Kinney beat me.
Wow.
So here I am with $50, and Lucky said to Deal it to him here. I dealt to him, pick up my hand, and he got blackjack.
Oh, man.

So now, I go to one of the guys in the band and I asked him to loan me $5. At that time, I was drinking Seagram's Seven. So I got off after the show, and I'm really down in the dumps, and I really feel awful because my wife thinks I'm coming home with this money to go buy these
new suits, and I ain't got a dime. So I borrow five dollars from this guy in the band; I forgot who it was, and I stopped in the whiskey store and bought me a pint of Seagram's Seven.

So when I got to the door, at home, my wife greeted me with a big smile on her face, and says, 'Well, we'll get up tomorrow morning and we'll do this and do that and then go to F&F and see about those suits for you' - and I said, 'There will be no suits' -- and she bust out in tears and said, 'Oh, no, not again!', and I said, 'Yep, I lost'. She said, 'When are you going to stop?'; I said, 'I don't know, but I got to stop, because all I'm doing is going downhill'.

And I think that was the thing that started me on my way to stop gambling. Because I saw my wife crying and looked at myself because I used to loved clothes, and I used to dress nice, and here I was, I was down to one suit, because all the rest of them were in pawn, and I did it all gambling.
Well, that's a beautiful story, man. There were sure some trying times during those days.
Yeah, they was.
And some good times, too.
Oh, yeah.
